{{recipesummary|category=Duck recipes|servings=3–4|time=1 hour to 90 minutes|difficulty=2
}}{{recipe}}| [[cookbook:Duck|Duck]] | [[cookbook:Poultry|Poultry]]
__NOTOC__
Long Island roast [[Cookbook:Duck|duckling]] is part of the regional cuisine of eastern Long Island, New York stemming from Long Island's thriving duck-farming industry which began in the late 19th century.<ref name="American duck farming">[http://www.foodreference.com/html/fducks.html Info on American duck farming on the Food Reference website]</ref> 

According to Alton Brown, host of the Food Network's ''Good Eats'', duck farming got its start on Long Island after an American businessman touring China in 1873 bought 25 white pekin ducks and shipped them to Long Island. Only nine survived the trip but those nine reproduced quickly and their descendants eventually found themselves on Long Island's numerous duck farms.<ref name= "What's Up, Duck (part one)">[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QSO_Ej2WwZU Part one of the ''Good Eats'' episode titled ''What's Up, Duck?'']</ref><ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Frn-M8HnlP0 Part two of the ''Good Eats'' episode titled ''What's Up, Duck?'']</ref>

White pekins (also called Long Island pekins) now represent 95% of the ducks sold and consumed in the US<ref>[http://www.mapleleaffarms.com/46#q13 Info on white pekin ducks on the Maple Farms website]</ref> and are raised on farms in many parts of that country.<ref>[http://metzerfarms.com The Mertzer Farms home page]</ref><ref>[http://duckhavenfarm.com The Duck Haven Farm home page]</ref><ref>[http://www.roastgoose.com The Schlitz Foods home page]</ref>

According to Brown, many people shy away from cooking whole ducks because of their high fat content.<ref name="What's Up, Duck (part one)"/> Fortunately, there are cooking methods for removing the excess fat.<ref>[http://www.thecitycook.com/cooking/recipes/data/000103 Info on roasting duck on The City Cook website]</ref>

White pekin meat has a mild flavor and, if served skinless, is lower in fat and calories than skinless chicken breast.<ref>[http://www.foodreference.com/html/fducks.html Info on white pekins on the Food Reference website]</ref> Farmers slaughter these birds after six to eight weeks of growth when the meat is at its most tender.<ref name="American duck farming"/>

This recipe utilizes a vertical roasting method to drain the fat away from the duck.

== Ingredients ==
* 1 whole [[Cookbook:Duck|pekin duckling]] (3–6 [[Cookbook:Pound|lbs]], 1.5–3 [[Cookbook:Kg|kg]])
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]]
* [[Cookbook:Pepper|Pepper]]
* Butter-flavored [[Cookbook:Cooking Spray|nonstick spray]]

== Preparation ==
# Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to [[Cookbook:Oven temperatures|450 °F]].  
# Rinse and wipe duckling, removing giblets.
# Set bird aside in an airy place to allow the skin to dry.
# Rub inside cavity with salt and pepper.
# Insert vertical oven roaster (used for "beer can chicken") into bird, and prop it upright.
# Coat bird on all sides with butter-flavored spray and sprinkle salt and pepper lightly over the skin.
# Place bird and vertical roaster into a large roasting pan (use a wire rack insert if you have one) and add ½ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] water to the bottom of the pan.  
# Leave bird in oven for 30 minutes, then reduce heat to [[Cookbook:Oven temperatures|325 °F]] until done. No need to prick skin or baste bird, as the fat slowly [[Cookbook:Rendering|renders]] off leaving a wonderful crispy skin. Keep the bottom of the roasting pan covered with water to prevent smoking.
# Pour off fat and save, reserving drippings and liquid from the roasting pan.

==Notes, tips, and variations== 
*Serve with brown [[Cookbook:Rice|rice]], [[cookbook:Rice Pilaf|rice pilaf]] or baked [[Cookbook:Sweet Potato|sweet potatoes]]. Cherry sauce and wild rice are also traditional.
*Use the duck fat to cook sliced [[Cookbook:Potato|potatoes]] or to make [[cookbook:Duck Confit|duck confit]].
*The fat and liver can be cooked together to make a very tasty paté so don't throw any of it out.
